content: The implementation of recommendations can influence outcomes, and adopting Option B+ for HIV treatment will likely require increased resources, particularly in the short term. However, the overall benefits of Option B+ are considered to outweigh potential harms. A cost-modeling analysis estimated that maintaining a woman on Option B+ for five years would cost approximately $2,069, including expenses for drugs, diagnostics, and service delivery. The incremental cost of transitioning from Option B to Option B+ was relatively low, ranging from $92 to $605, depending on baseline CD4 count and breastfeeding status. Multiple model-based analyses have supported the cost-effectiveness of strategies to prevent mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV, with Options B and B+ often being cost-saving or highly cost-effective compared to Option A. When considering broader outcomes, such as maternal health, prevention of HIV transmission in future pregnancies, and horizontal transmission prevention, Option B+ has been found to be highly cost-effective compared to Option B. A qualitative review of the acceptability of Option B+ revealed high acceptance of lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART) among pregnant and breastfeeding women and healthcare providers. While some women expressed concerns about drug toxicity for themselves and their children, they generally valued the health benefits and the ability to protect their children and partners from HIV. Early program experiences in South Africa indicated that same-day ART initiation (starting ART on the day of HIV diagnosis) was acceptable to pregnant women, particularly in settings where women were already aware of their HIV status, had high levels of treatment literacy, and could access support services. In contrast, same-day ART initiation in Malawi was associated with high rates of early loss to follow-up, with many women failing to return for a second visit. The recommendation to initiate ART for all adults with HIV, regardless of CD4 count, is expected to improve the acceptability of ART for pregnant and breastfeeding women by normalizing what was previously stigmatized. A simplified and harmonized approach to ART for pregnant and non-pregnant adults will also promote health equity. Program managers must address several issues when implementing the policy of providing lifelong ART to all pregnant and breastfeeding women. These include ensuring the quality of HIV testing, determining the appropriate timing for ART initiation in newly diagnosed women, and maintaining continuity of ART services during the postpartum period. Ideally, ART for pregnant and breastfeeding women should be delivered within maternal, newborn, and child health clinics by integrating HIV and antenatal care. Integrated services benefit mothers and are likely feasible in settings with a high burden of HIV infection. However, achieving integration will depend on the availability of resources, including staff time and physical space. A retrospective cohort study in Malawi found that 45% of women who started ART in antenatal care clinics were referred to separate ART services shortly after delivery. There is no established model for transitioning mothers on ART out of maternal and child health services, but a report from South Africa highlighted the importance of addressing this potential additional loss point in the PMTCT cascade. A retrospective review of women referred to ART clinics postpartum found that up to 25% did not remain in care five months after referral. Beyond clinical service delivery, national programs must strengthen data systems to track women on ART across multiple delivery sites and implement targeted interventions to improve adherence and retention, such as community support and peer counselors. Significant knowledge gaps remain regarding the optimal implementation of Option B+ to improve retention and follow-up for mothers and infants. For example, further assessment is needed to determine the effectiveness of integrating antiretroviral drug delivery into antenatal and maternal, neonatal, and childcare services compared to referral to ART clinics. Adolescents and young women living with HIV face unique challenges in preventing HIV transmission to their children and addressing their own health needs, including poor access to reproductive health services, low uptake of testing, and poor retention in care. Operational research is urgently needed to identify the drivers of poor outcomes among adolescents, define adolescent-friendly maternal and newborn health services, and develop strategies to improve retention in care. The review of evidence, programmatic data, and operational considerations has led to a separate recommendation for adolescents living with HIV. This highlights the importance of initiating ART and providing treatment and care tailored to adolescents. In 2013, an estimated 1 million adolescents (aged 10–19 years) were living with HIV globally. HIV-related deaths among adolescents have tripled since 2000, making HIV the second leading cause of death among adolescents worldwide. Adolescents are underserved by current HIV services, have significantly worse access to ART than adults, and face high risks of loss to follow-up and suboptimal adherence. They also require comprehensive care, including psychosocial support and sexual and reproductive health services. Barriers to accessing essential health and support services include policy and legal restrictions related to the age of consent. The 2013 WHO antiretroviral guidelines aligned the clinical and immunological criteria for ART eligibility among adolescents with those for adults, recommending treatment initiation for WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 disease or a CD4 count at or below 500 cells/mm³. This alignment aimed to simplify programming and avoid delays in treatment initiation. However, there are limitations in extrapolating evidence from adults to adolescents, and uncertainty remains about the potential benefits of immediate ART initiation for adolescent health outcomes, given the challenges of achieving long-term adherence and retention in this age group. Adolescents living with HIV are less adherent to treatment than adults and younger children. Effective interventions and services to support adherence among adolescents, including community interventions and peer educators, are required. Earlier ART initiation among adolescents is likely feasible within existing health systems, but increased patient enrollments will place additional demands on supply chains and provider workloads. Developing adolescent-friendly health services and emphasizing adherence and retention support will be critical to ensuring timely diagnosis and treatment for adolescents. For children living with HIV, the 2015 recommendations align with those for adults and adolescents, advocating for ART initiation regardless of clinical or immunological status. Infants and young children living with HIV face exceptionally high risks of poor outcomes, with up to 52% of children born with HIV dying before the age of two without intervention. Improved access to early infant diagnosis has increased the identification of infants living with HIV, but ART initiation rates among this group remain suboptimal. Diagnosing and retaining children in care is particularly challenging due to their dependence on caregivers. Expanding ART to all children living with HIV is expected to increase equity and be well-accepted. Implementing this recommendation is likely feasible, as most children identified as living with HIV would already be eligible for ART based on 2013 criteria. However, increased numbers of children receiving ART may lead to higher demands on supply chain systems and provider workloads. Strategies to improve retention in care and support adherence will be essential as ART is expanded to all children.
